A lesion is any area of tissue or organ in your body that has been damaged, changed, or made abnormal — whether by injury, disease, infection, or any other harmful process.

Think of it this way: your body, when healthy, has tissues and organs that look and work in a specific, normal way. The moment any part of that tissue gets damaged or structurally altered in an abnormal way, that affected spot is called a lesion.

It is essentially a doctor's umbrella word for almost any abnormal spot, patch, sore, wound, growth, or area of damage found anywhere in the body.

This is important to understand clearly:

  • A lesion is not a disease itself. It is the physical sign or mark left behind by a disease, injury, or abnormal process.
  • A lesion is not always something you can see. Some lesions are visible on the skin; others are deep inside the brain, lungs, liver, or bones, and can only be detected through scans or tests.
  • A lesion is not always serious. A small pimple is technically a lesion. So is a life-threatening brain tumor. The word carries no built-in judgment about severity — it just means "abnormal area of tissue."

Lesions can occur in virtually any part of the body, because every part of the body is made of tissue. Here are the most commonly talked-about locations:

Skin lesions — These are the most familiar. Anything that causes an abnormal spot or change on your skin qualifies. This includes cuts, burns, rashes, blisters, ulcers, moles, warts, acne, cold sores, and skin cancers.

Brain lesions — Areas of damage inside the brain. These can be caused by strokes (where blood supply is cut off, killing brain cells), tumors, multiple sclerosis (MS), traumatic brain injuries (like a hard blow to the head), or infections. Brain lesions are serious because the brain controls everything.

Bone lesions — Abnormal areas within a bone, which can result from tumors (benign or cancerous), infections, or cysts.

Lung lesions — Often seen on chest X-rays or CT scans as abnormal spots, which could be infections, scarring, cysts, or tumors.

Liver, kidney, and other organ lesions — Abnormal spots on internal organs, often discovered incidentally during imaging for something else.

Spinal cord lesions — Damage to the spinal cord from injury, MS, or disease, which can affect movement and sensation throughout the body.

Oral lesions — Sores, ulcers, or abnormal patches inside the mouth (like canker sores or oral cancer patches).

Doctors classify lesions in several useful ways:

By whether they are harmful or not:

  • Benign lesions — Harmless and non-cancerous. A common mole, a skin tag, or a benign cyst are all benign lesions. They may not need treatment at all.
  • Malignant lesions — Cancerous. These are dangerous, can invade surrounding tissue, and can spread to other parts of the body. A melanoma (skin cancer) is a malignant lesion.
  • Precancerous lesions — Not yet cancer, but abnormal enough that they could become cancerous over time. These are important to monitor or treat early.

By what caused them:

  • Traumatic lesions — Caused by physical injury (a cut, a bruise, a burn).
  • Infectious lesions — Caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites (a cold sore caused by the herpes virus, a skin abscess from bacteria).
  • Inflammatory lesions — Caused by the body's immune response reacting abnormally (the red, inflamed patches in psoriasis or eczema).
  • Vascular lesions — Caused by problems with blood vessels (a stroke lesion in the brain, a hemangioma on the skin).
  • Neoplastic lesions — Caused by abnormal cell growth, which can be benign or malignant (tumors, cysts, warts from HPV).
  • Degenerative lesions — Caused by the breakdown of tissue over time due to aging or chronic disease.

By size and appearance (for skin lesions especially):

Doctors are very precise about describing skin lesions by their physical characteristics:

  • A macule is a flat, discoloured patch (like a freckle).
  • A papule is a small, raised, solid bump (like a pimple without pus).
  • A vesicle is a small, fluid-filled blister (like a chickenpox spot).
  • A pustule is a raised bump filled with pus (like a whitehead).
  • An ulcer is an open sore where the surface tissue has broken down.
  • A nodule is a larger, deeper solid lump beneath the skin.

These specific terms all fall under the umbrella of the word "lesion."
How Doctors Actually Use This Word

When a doctor says "lesion," they are using a deliberately neutral and precise term that does not prejudge what the abnormality is. It simply says: "Something here is not normal, and we need to investigate further."

For example:

  • A radiologist looking at a brain scan might report: "There is a lesion in the left temporal lobe." — This tells the referring doctor that something abnormal was found, but more investigation (like a biopsy) is needed to determine exactly what it is.
  • A dermatologist examining your skin might say: "I'd like to take a closer look at that lesion on your arm." — They are not yet saying it is cancer; they are simply identifying it as something abnormal that warrants examination.

This neutral quality is one of the reasons the word is so useful in medicine — it is descriptive without being prematurely conclusive.

Here are real-world things you are likely familiar with, now understood through the lens of this word:

What you call itWhat it is as a lesion
A cold soreA viral skin lesion caused by the herpes simplex virus
A pimpleAn inflammatory skin lesion
A cancerous moleA malignant skin lesion
A stroke "scar" in the brainA vascular brain lesion
An MS plaque in the brainA demyelinating brain lesion
A diabetic foot ulcerA chronic skin lesion
A chickenpox spotAn infectious skin lesion

Very occasionally, especially in older legal writing (particularly in civil law traditions), the word "lesion" can refer to harm or loss suffered by one party in a contract — for instance, if someone is taken advantage of and suffers a financial injury due to an unfair agreement. However, this usage is rare today, and in nearly all modern contexts, when someone says "lesion," they mean the medical meaning described throughout this explanation.
The Single Best Way to Remember It

A lesion = any abnormal, damaged, or structurally altered spot in body tissue, regardless of where it is, what caused it, or how serious it is.

It is a doctor's precise, neutral, all-purpose word for saying: "This part of the body is not as it should be."
